newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Rights group to challenge Guatemalan amnesty law.
newsitem.headline: Rights group to challenge Guatemalan amnesty law.

text.p: Human rights activists said on Friday they would legally challenge an amnesty law passed by the Guatemalan Congress this week.
"We are confident that the unconstitutionality suit will be succesful," Karen Fischer, spokeswoman for the Alliance Against Impunity, told Reuters.

The law, passed by a strong majority in Congress on Wednesday, provides limited amnesty for combatants on both sides of the 36-year civil war in which an estimated 100,000 people died and another 40,000 disappeared.
While the government has promoted the law as a limited amnesty for political and war-related crimes, critics say it will allow those responsible for killings to go unpunished.
Fischer said the rights group will file its lawsuit as soon as President Alvaro Arzu signs the law.
The amnesty must go into effect before commanders of the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) can return from exile to attend the Dec. 29 signing of a peace treaty.
By granting amnesty for political crimes such as sedition and rebellion, the law converts guerrillas from wanted people into ordinary citizens.
Both URNG rebels and army personnel would receive amnesty for common crimes committed in the war, such as threats, damages, fires, explosives or the falsification of documents.

Rights activists argue the law does not specifically exclude kidnappings and murders from the amnesty. They fear army officers accused of ordering the murder of opponents and intellectuals would never stand trial.
Fischer said the lawsuit will challenge the new law's constitutionality on a technical basis, because the president sent the bill to Congress without the obligatory signature of a cabinet minister.
According to Fischer the law is also unconstitutional because it defines some common crimes as political crimes.
